title: The Exception Code Every Core Throw Carries
hints: Every throw in the core carries a unique ten-digit integer exception code, by convention the unix timestamp the throw was written at. It is the second constructor argument of a PHP exception, and the code: named argument where a core exception class takes the parameter somewhere else.
A fixture is read exactly as production code is, so a throw written for one needs its code too.

hints.text: CI=true ./Build/Scripts/runTests.sh -s checkIntegrityPhp is what reports it, as Undefined, Duplicated or Malformed Exception Codes detected, each with the file and the line. Malformed is the code that is not an integer of that length. Which directories it reads is in the suite's own entry, which typo3_test_run_guide returns.
A code taken from an exception that was caught is left alone: getCode() in the code argument passes.
CI=true ./Build/Scripts/runTests.sh -s checkExceptionCodes is what reports it, over every *.php below typo3/, and it stops at the first throw it finds without a code.

hints: The suite named for listing exception codes checks nothing: -s listExceptionCodes prints them as JSON and exits successfully whether one is missing or used twice. It is how to see which codes are taken, and the suites above are what confirm a throw has one.
The core's own pre-merge pipeline runs the checking suite, so a throw written without a code fails there before a person reads the patch.

title: Which PHP a TYPO3 Version Requires and Is Tested On
hints: The php constraint typo3/cms-core declares in its own composer.json is the requirement, and it is the only one of the three numbers here that is: Composer refuses to install the core on an interpreter outside it. A project narrowing it further supports less than the core does, for no reason the core gave.

config.platform.php in the core repository pins its own dependency resolution to a version at the floor of that constraint, so a Composer run there resolves as if it were on the oldest interpreter the core admits, whatever the machine runs. A project gets that property only by setting the key itself; without it, a container on a newer PHP resolves dependencies the declared floor may not be able to install.

The -p option of Build/Scripts/runTests.sh names the interpreters a branch runs its own suites on, and without it the script takes the floor. That is the core testing itself: it says what the branch is exercised against, not what the TYPO3 project supports an installation on.

hints.text: The constraint is PHP ^8.1, config.platform.php is PHP 8.1.1, and the suites run on PHP 8.1 through PHP 8.5.
The constraint is PHP ^8.2, config.platform.php is PHP 8.2.0, and the suites run on PHP 8.2 through PHP 8.6.

The constraint is PHP ^8.5, config.platform.php is PHP 8.5.0, and the suites run on PHP 8.5 and PHP 8.6. The development line raises its floor ahead of the release it becomes, so what installs there is an interpreter no released line requires.

hints: A container's interpreter is chosen before there is an installation to ask about it, and nothing afterwards revisits the number. Choose it against the constraint and the tested range of the target line rather than against what the machine already has, and keep the declared floor and the interpreter every environment runs in a relation you can name: a floor below what is ever executed is a claim no run tests.

title: Which PHP a Backported Patch Has to Parse Under
appliesTo: which PHP syntax may I write
parse error on the release branch
hints: The interpreter a patch has to parse under is the floor of the oldest branch its Releases: trailer names, not the floor of the branch it is written on. Nothing on the branch you push from reads that trailer, so newer syntax passes every suite there and becomes a parse error when the backport lands.
A parse error takes the whole file with it, so the class stops existing rather than reporting, and it surfaces in front of whoever does the cherry-pick instead of in the pipeline the author watched.

Read the floor off each branch the trailer names rather than remembering it: the php key of that branch's own composer.json is the requirement, and the php-versions hint is the same question asked per line.

Running the file under that floor is what catches it, and reading the diff is not. The -p option of Build/Scripts/runTests.sh names the interpreter a suite runs on, and php -l on the changed files under the same interpreter is the cheap half of it.

hints.text: Instantiation without parentheses — new X()->method() — is the one such form the core writes today: the development line uses it throughout and no released line parses it. Asymmetric visibility and property hooks are the other candidates and occur nowhere in the core yet, so the rule above is what to apply rather than a list of features to remember.

Parenthesising it is not the stable form. The development line's Build/php-cs-fixer/config.php enables new_expression_parentheses, whose default removes them, so -s cgl rewrites (new X())->method() straight back to the syntax the older branch cannot read. Binding the instance to a variable first is the form both lines keep.

title: Testing a Value Rather Than Its Falsiness
hints: empty() tests falsiness rather than a value against the type it is expected to have: 0, '0', '', null, false and [] all satisfy it. So the condition names none of them, and a value arriving wrong as one of the others reads as the case the code was written for — nothing raises, and the branch taken is the intended one.

What replaces it is the check the expected type makes: ($x ?? false) where a bool is meant, ($x ?? null) !== null for an object that may be absent, $x !== [] for an array, $x !== '' for a string. The type decides which, so the substitution is a reading of what the value is and never mechanical.
!isset($x) || empty($x) is that one check written twice, and it collapses to !($x ?? false) rather than to the empty() half.

The core's own code is full of empty() and nothing there fails on it: Build/phpstan/phpstan.neon runs at level 5, and none of the rules it adds is about this call. So a call standing beside the line being changed is a finding to raise rather than a local style to keep, which core-static-analysis says the analysis will not raise for you.
